thread.title: FANG Tumbles But Microsoft Stands Strong - Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT) | Seeking Alpha

author: Julian Lin
title: FANG Tumbles But Microsoft Stands Strong - Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT) | Seeking Alpha
text:
Some have bled more than others. Microsoft ( MSFT ) has shown in recent months why being responsible with free cash flow and choosing to return cash to shareholders is an important sign of maturity. The company's financials continue to be very strong and it also boasts a strong balance sheet. Shares are a buy with around 20% upside in the next 12 months.
When Will The Others See The Light? The last couple months have been harsh on tech stocks - but some have been hit harder than others. It would appear that high-flying tech stocks like "FANG" have been hit among the hardest.
As we can see below: MSFT has strongly outperformed FANG amidst the sell-off:
(Chart by Author)
The problem does not appear to be due to financial results; FANG's recent quarter showed continued bite in earnings growth. The problem in my opinion is due to something else not frequently discussed in the growth sector: shareholder capital return programs. FANG is notorious for being lackluster in returning cash to shareholders. Amazon ( AMZN ) and Netflix ( NFLX ) do not generate significant free cash flow and thus their inclusion is unintentional (but not excused). Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG ) (NASDAQ: GOOGL ) continues to pay no dividend and repurchase fewer shares than it issues despite very strong free cash flows, leading to a cash hoard over $100 billion and growing. GOOGL is becoming Apple 2.0 ( AAPL ) from a couple years ago, but I digress. Facebook ( FB ), my top pick in the sector and overall, is arguably the strongest among the 4, as it has put 100% of free cash flows this year towards share repurchases. Even so, I argue that it should be paying a dividend and that there is no reason to be holding a $40 billion cash position with no debt.
MSFT on the other hand displays great maturity in a sector in apparently great need for strong role models. MSFT pays a strong dividend which it has grown for 14 consecutive years. In addition to the $3.2 billion in dividends it paid last quarter, MSFT also repurchased $3.7 billion in stock. While not totaling 100% of free cash flows (which would be ideal), this is very impressive and a wise decision by management.
Some investors have hard, negative feelings about share repurchases and, even "worse," dividends. The argument makes sense intuitively: aren't these uses of capital very poor in comparison with reinvesting the cash back into the business (innovation)? The problem with this thinking may arise from becoming too used to expecting strong growth forever. Strong companies in strong growth markets will be able to deploy great amounts of money at high returns of capital during their early periods. I have no argument about reinvesting cash at high ROI. These investments tend to be included in the "R&D" line item on the income statement. However, every company inevitably reaches a point where they simply are unable to find investment opportunities for which they can deploy all their excess cash at high ROI. It would be a very poor decision to reinvest "for the sake of growth," which would involve reinvesting cash flows at poor ROI, so that is off the table.
FB, GOOGL, and MSFT have already reached this point many years ago. This is evidenced by their large cash hoards - as discussed above, FB and GOOGL have large cash piles at around $40 billion and $100 billion respectively, and MSFT had over $70 billion in net cash as of the most recent quarter. While I agree that cash that could be reinvested at high ROI back into the business should not be used for dividends and share repurchases, I however am adamant in disagreeing that cash which has no such investment opportunity should be allowed to accumulate in what are ultimately low-yielding checking accounts. Growth investors should not consider 1% yielding bank accounts to be a strong option of growth - thus that leaves only three alternatives: dividends, share repurchases, and M&A.
M&A could sometimes be a good investment choice; however, as we are talking about billions upon billions of dollars, I should point out that high dollar-value acquisitions tend to not work out . For example, to this day, it is still not clear if MSFT did not simply overpay when it bought LinkedIn for over $26 billion. Further, if it is able to eventually prove profitable synergies from the acquisition in the future, if ever, this would also be an exception to the rule rather than the norm.
This means that by process of elimination, we are left with two choices: dividends and share repurchases. The decision between the two is quite complicated but usually goes along the lines of prioritizing share repurchases when shares are below a certain price threshold, or otherwise more rapidly increasing the dividend.
This inevitably leads to some combination of the two comprised of a steadily growing dividend.
That explains why MSFT's decision to aggressively return cash to shareholders is very wise, and potentially why it has strongly outperformed FANG. Readers who still have doubts are encouraged to leave a comment in the comment section.
Firing On All Cylinders MSFT continues to fire on all cylinders, validating its status as a high octane dividend growth stock. MSFT grew revenues at 18% and EPS at 33% YOY:
( FY2019 Q1 Presentation )
Investors should focus on the rapidly improving financials of its "intelligent cloud" division:
(FY2019 Q1 Presentation)
This segment is highlighted by the strength of Azure, which saw revenue growth slow, but still come in very strong at 76%. I don't think anyone can complain about such impressive growth:
(FY2019 Q1 Presentation)
Due to the rapid adoption of Azure, MSFT continues to see operating margins for this segment increase:
(FY2019 Q1 Presentation)
While the Intelligent Cloud division may be the company's brightest growth point, most probably know MSFT best for its "Productivity and Business Processes" division. This division is anchored by the Office 365, LinkedIn, and Dynamics 365 products. In addition to benefiting from adding new customers altogether, MSFT is also seeing a shift from upfront-fee users towards recurring annual subscribers. As we can see below, these products saw very strong double-digit top-line growth:
(FY2019 Q1 Presentation)
The last division is "More Personal Computing." This division is considered its least favorable as it isn't very "SAASy." In other words, the revenues are not growing as fast and are not as recurring. Nonetheless, MSFT continues to show that its Xbox and operating system products continue to be in high demand:
(FY2019 Q1 Presentation)
All in all, MSFT continues to perform strong financially - how much are we paying for these earnings?
Valuation and Price Target If you use typical business websites in determining MSFT's P/E ratio, you are likely to land with something around 45, which would make shares appear expensive. We however should adjust for one-time tax charges related to tax reform of last year. MSFT has trailing 12-month operating income before taxes of $38.7 billion. Management has guided for a 17% full-year tax rate, making for $32.12 billion in trailing net income. Based on 7.77 billion shares outstanding, this represents trailing EPS of $4.13. This means that at recent prices, MSFT trades for just under 27 times earnings. Considering that it has just grown EPS over 30% YOY, this is a very reasonable valuation. However, it gets better: MSFT, like FB and GOOGL, benefits from a potential balance sheet catalyst due to its large net cash position.
With over $70 billion in net cash, this means that MSFT will be able to not only repurchase many shares in the future, but also potentially even take on debt. I believe that it can take on net debt equal to at least 1 times EBITDA, which would be $52 billion for the trailing 12 months. Adjusting for net cash, MSFT sells for about 24.7 times earnings, and adjusting for potential debt, sells for 23 times earnings. These are very reasonable multiples considering its strong growth potential. Previously I have given a 12-month price target of $136, or 33 times trailing earnings. However, given that valuations have dropped across the board especially in the tech sector, I need to revise this estimate downward slightly. My 12-month price target for MSFT is now $133, which I believe the company will be able to achieve through continued EPS growth. I rate shares a buy - but should note that there appear to also be many appealing alternatives in the tech sector potentially trading at more attractive valuations.
Risks As stated above, MSFT has performed strongly, which I believe is very much due to its capital allocation policies. This however could also suggest that the company is now valued richly compared to the rest of the tech sector, and thus may underperform as other names see more meaningful multiple revaluations upwards. That said, I view the entire group to be so cheap that MSFT should nonetheless still generate strong returns long term even if it is not necessarily the best pick in the group.
While its $70 billion net cash position is a potential catalyst, share repurchases are however probably a best-case scenario, and the longer management decides to maintain the position means greater the risk that it does other things, such as M&A. While acquiring another company right now may not prove to be so bad considering lower valuations across the board, there is risk that MSFT may do so at a high premium (like it did with LinkedIn) or wait until valuations have been restored (and again would need to pay a high valuation). MSFT has done high-value acquisitions in the past and thus this risk is particularly higher here than with FB or GOOGL. I hope to see it more aggressively increase its dividend or share repurchases moving forward.
MSFT faces potential competition in both cloud (notably from AMZN) and office products (notably from GOOGL). While all three are right now experiencing strong growth due to an untapped and growing market, they will inevitably at some point begin competing with each other. At this point, we may see margins compress as they are no longer able to exert the same pricing pressure as before. That said, there is no indication that this time has yet arrived.
Conclusion MSFT has that rare combination of strong growth and strong capital allocators at the helm. Shares are reasonably priced in their own right, making them a buy even though there may be cheaper alternatives. Shares have about 20% upside in the next 12 months.
